name: Kansas

events.title: Statehood
events.text: Kansas became the 34th state on January 29, 1861.

events.title: 1870 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1870 census, Kansas's House delegation grew from 1 to 3 seats.

events.title: Statewide (general ticket) elections
events.text: In the 43rd Congress (1873–1875), Kansas elected all of its representatives statewide on a general ticket instead of by district.

events.title: 1880 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1880 census, Kansas's House delegation grew from 3 to 7 seats.

events.title: Some members elected at-large
events.text: In the 48th Congress (1883–1885), Kansas elected 4 of its representatives statewide (at-large) and the rest by district.

events.title: 1890 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1890 census, Kansas's House delegation grew from 7 to 8 seats.

events.title: Some members elected at-large
events.text: In the 53rd through 59th Congresses (1893–1907), Kansas elected one of its representatives statewide (at-large) and the rest by district.

events.title: 1900 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1900 census, Kansas kept 8 seats in the House.

events.title: 1910 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1910 census, Kansas kept 8 seats in the House.

events.title: 1930 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1930 census, Kansas's House delegation shrank from 8 to 7 seats.

events.title: 1940 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1940 census, Kansas's House delegation shrank from 7 to 6 seats.

events.title: 1950 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1950 census, Kansas kept 6 seats in the House.

events.title: 1960 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1960 census, Kansas's House delegation shrank from 6 to 5 seats.

events.title: 1970 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1970 census, Kansas kept 5 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 1980 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1980 census, Kansas kept 5 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 1990 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1990 census, Kansas's House delegation shrank from 5 to 4 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 2000 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2000 census, Kansas kept 4 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 2010 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2010 census, Kansas kept 4 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: Essex v. Kobach
events.text: The legislature could not agree on a congressional plan after the 2010 census, so a federal court drew Kansas's four districts itself, imposing its plan on June 7, 2012.

events.title: Map upheld
events.text: The legislature overrode the governor's veto to enact a new congressional map. The Kansas Supreme Court upheld it in May 2022 in Rivera v. Schwab.

events.title: 2020 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2020 census, Kansas kept 4 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: Mid-decade redraw does not advance
events.text: In fall 2025, legislative leaders sought a special session to redraw the map mid-decade, but the petition fell short of two-thirds support in the House. In January 2026, the House speaker said the votes to override a promised veto were not there.

compactnessNote: Polsby-Popper compactness (4π × area ÷ perimeter²) measured on the projected district shapes. It describes shape only: coastlines, rivers and county lines lower it too, so a low score is not evidence of intent. "Irregular" marks the least compact 5% of district shapes in each census era nationally.

c044.text: New map drawn after the 1870 census, which raised Kansas's seats from 1 to 3. It was first used in the 1874 election.

c049.text: New map drawn after the 1880 census, which raised Kansas's seats from 3 to 7. It was first used in the 1884 election.

c056.text: Kansas's district lines were redrawn between censuses, first used in the 1898 election. The reason has not been researched yet.

c060.text: Kansas's district lines were redrawn between censuses, first used in the 1906 election. The reason has not been researched yet.

c073.text: New map drawn after the 1930 census, which cut Kansas's seats from 8 to 7. It was first used in the 1932 election.

c078.text: New map drawn after the 1940 census, which cut Kansas's seats from 7 to 6. It was first used in the 1942 election.

c088.text: New map drawn after the 1960 census, which cut Kansas's seats from 6 to 5. It was first used in the 1962 election.

c090.text: Kansas's district lines were redrawn between censuses, first used in the 1966 election. The reason has not been researched yet.

c093.text: New map drawn after the 1970 census, which left Kansas with 5 seats. It was first used in the 1972 election.

c098.text: New map drawn after the 1980 census, which left Kansas with 5 seats. It was first used in the 1982 election.

c103.text: New map drawn after the 1990 census, which cut Kansas's seats from 5 to 4. It was first used in the 1992 election.

c108.text: New map drawn after the 2000 census, which left Kansas with 4 seats. It was first used in the 2002 election.

c113.text: New map following: Essex v. Kobach. The legislature could not agree on a congressional plan after the 2010 census, so a federal court drew Kansas's four districts itself, imposing its plan on June 7, 2012.

c118.text: New map drawn after the 2020 census, which left Kansas with 4 seats. It was first used in the 2022 election.
